title: Random Walks, Brownian Motion & Martingales
tagline: The math of how prices move randomly through time — the language of quant research.

concept.analogy: Picture a drunk walking home from a bar, taking each step left or right at random. Where will they be after 100 steps? You can't predict the exact spot, but you can describe the distribution — centered where they started, spreading out over time. Asset prices, over short horizons, behave a lot like this random walk; the math of the drunkard's walk is the math of price uncertainty.
paragraphs: A stochastic process is a sequence of random variables indexed by time — a model of something evolving randomly. The simplest is the random walk: at each step, add a random increment (e.g., +1 or −1 with equal probability). Its key properties: the expected position stays at the start (zero drift), but the variance grows linearly with the number of steps, so the typical distance from the start grows like √t. That √t scaling is everywhere in finance.

Brownian motion (the Wiener process) is the continuous-time limit of a random walk: increments are independent, normally distributed with variance proportional to the time elapsed, and paths are continuous. It's the building block of continuous-time finance. Geometric Brownian Motion (GBM) models prices as always positive with log-returns following Brownian motion with drift — the basis of the Black-Scholes model.

A martingale is a process whose expected future value, given everything known now, equals its current value: E[X_{t+1} | history] = X_t. It formalizes a 'fair game' — no predictable drift. The efficient-market idea that you can't predict the next move from the past is a martingale statement, and many fair-value constructs (like a well-built microprice) are designed to be martingales.

You don't need to derive Itô's lemma to do well in most HFT interviews (it matters more for derivatives/pricing roles), but you must be fluent in: random walks, the √t scaling of volatility, expectation/variance of sums, what 'martingale' means, and why returns (not prices) are usually modeled as roughly independent.
points: Random walk: independent increments; zero drift but variance grows ∝ t (typical distance ∝ √t).
Brownian motion: continuous-time limit; independent Gaussian increments, variance ∝ time.
GBM: prices stay positive, log-returns are Brownian with drift — basis of Black-Scholes.
Martingale: E[future | now] = now — a 'fair game' with no predictable drift.
Volatility scales with √t — a cornerstone fact for risk and option intuition.
concept.keyIdea: Prices over short horizons resemble a random walk: unpredictable in direction but with uncertainty (volatility) growing as √t. Brownian motion is its continuous-time version, and 'martingale' is the precise statement that the next move isn't predictable from the past.

deepDive.intro: The facts and intuitions you must have at your fingertips.

steps.title: Random walk: mean and variance
steps.detail: Let S_n = X_1 + … + X_n with each X_i = ±1 equally likely (mean 0, variance 1). Then E[S_n] = 0 and Var(S_n) = n (variances of independent variables add). So the standard deviation is √n — after 100 steps you're typically ~10 away, not 100. This √t growth of spread is the single most important takeaway.

steps.title: Why √t (volatility scaling)
steps.detail: Because variances add for independent increments, variance ∝ time, and standard deviation (volatility) ∝ √time. To convert daily vol to annual: multiply by √252 (trading days). This is why a 1%-daily-vol asset has ~16% annual vol (√252 ≈ 16), not 252%.

steps.title: Brownian motion and GBM
steps.detail: Brownian motion W_t: W_0 = 0, independent increments, W_t − W_s ~ Normal(0, t−s), continuous paths. GBM models price as dS = μS dt + σS dW, i.e., percentage returns (not absolute) are Brownian — keeping prices positive and returns scale-free. Black-Scholes assumes GBM.

steps.title: Martingales and fair games
steps.detail: X is a martingale if E[X_{t+1} | F_t] = X_t (F_t = info up to t). A symmetric random walk is a martingale; a betting game with zero edge is a martingale. 'You can't beat a martingale with a clever stopping rule' (optional stopping) underlies why naive timing strategies don't add EV. Markets being (near-)martingales after costs is why edges are so hard-won.

steps.title: What this buys you in practice
steps.detail: Risk: position risk over horizon t scales with σ√t — used for limits and sizing. Signals: a good fair-value estimate should be ~martingale (no leftover predictability), so any predictability is your alpha. Options intuition: time-value and the √t spreading of outcomes explain why longer-dated and higher-vol options cost more.

notes.title: Real prices aren't pure random walks
notes.detail: Empirically, returns have fat tails, volatility clusters (GARCH-like), and there are tiny short-horizon predictabilities (the HFT edge). The random walk / Brownian model is a baseline you deviate from deliberately — interviewers like when you know both the model and its limitations.

pitfalls: Scaling volatility linearly with time instead of with √t.
Confusing modeling prices vs. returns — returns (often log-returns) are what's modeled as ~independent.
Assuming a random walk implies prices are 'mean-reverting to the start' — a driftless walk has no pull back; spread just grows.
Overstating realism — real returns have fat tails and volatility clustering.

interviewQuestions.q: A symmetric random walk starts at 0, taking ±1 steps. After 100 steps, what's the expected position and the standard deviation of the position?
a: Each step has mean 0 and variance 1, and steps are independent. Expected position E[S_100] = 100 × 0 = 0 — there's no drift.
Variance adds: Var(S_100) = 100 × 1 = 100, so standard deviation = √100 = 10. So after 100 steps you're centered at 0 but typically about ±10 away — the hallmark √n spreading.
followups: What's the probability the walk is positive after 100 steps?
How does this connect to converting daily to annual volatility?

interviewQuestions.q: A stock has 1% daily volatility. Approximately what's its annualized volatility, and why?
a: Volatility scales with the square root of time (variance adds over independent periods, so std grows as √t). There are about 252 trading days in a year.
So annual vol ≈ daily vol × √252 ≈ 1% × 15.87 ≈ 16%. The key is √252 ≈ 16, NOT ×252. This √t scaling is one of the most-tested facts in quant interviews.

interviewQuestions.q: What is a martingale, and why is it relevant to building a fair-value estimate like the microprice?
a: A martingale is a process where the best forecast of the future value, given all current information, is just the current value: E[X_{t+1} | info now] = X_t. It's the formal notion of a 'fair game' with no predictable drift.

A good fair-value estimate should be (close to) a martingale: once you've incorporated all available information into your estimate, there should be no remaining predictable drift in it — if there were, you'd just fold that prediction into the estimate. So you build fair value (e.g., the Stoikov microprice) to be martingale-like, and then any genuine, exploitable predictability you find beyond it is, by definition, your alpha. It also explains why naive timing rules add no EV against a martingale (optional stopping).

interviewQuestions.q: What is a martingale, and why is the concept useful in trading and interviews?
a: A martingale is a process whose expected next value, given everything you know so far, equals its current value: E[X_{t+1} | history] = X_t. Informally, it's a 'fair game' — no drift up or down in expectation. A symmetric random walk and a fair-coin gambling bankroll are martingales; so, under risk-neutral pricing, are discounted asset prices.

It's useful because martingale properties let you compute expectations and prove 'you can't beat a fair game' results elegantly. The Optional Stopping Theorem says that for a martingale, under suitable conditions, the expected value at a stopping time equals the start value — which immediately solves many gambler's-ruin and hitting-time problems without messy summation. In trading, the martingale/efficient-market idea underlies why you can't predict a fair-game price's direction (only its variance grows with time), why a pure martingale strategy has zero expected profit, and the risk-neutral pricing of derivatives. Interviewers use it to test whether you recognize a fair game and avoid fallacies like 'it's due to go up.'
followups: State the Optional Stopping Theorem informally.
Why does a martingale betting system not beat the house?

problems.title: Volatility scaling with time (√t)
problems.statement: A stock's log-returns are i.i.d. with daily volatility (standard deviation) of 1%. Assuming returns are independent across days, what is the volatility over 4 days? Over a 256-trading-day year? Explain the √t scaling and why it's so fundamental, and one assumption that can break it.
problems.hint: Variances of independent increments add; standard deviation scales with the square root of the number of periods.
problems.tests: Variance additivity and the square-root-of-time rule.

approach: For independent increments, variances add: Var over n periods = n × (per-period variance). Standard deviation (volatility) therefore scales with √n. With daily vol σ_d = 1% = 0.01: over 4 days, vol = σ_d × √4 = 0.01 × 2 = 2%. Over 256 days, vol = 0.01 × √256 = 0.01 × 16 = 16% annualized.

This √t scaling is fundamental: it's why annualized vol = daily vol × √(trading days), why a random walk's spread widens like √t (not linearly), and why diffusion/Brownian motion has standard deviation proportional to √t. It directly informs position sizing, option pricing (vol scales with √(time-to-expiry)), and risk limits over different horizons.

Assumption that breaks it: independence (and identical distribution) of returns. If returns are autocorrelated — e.g., momentum (positive autocorrelation) makes multi-period variance grow faster than n, while mean-reversion (negative autocorrelation) makes it grow slower — the simple √t rule fails. Volatility clustering (today's vol predicts tomorrow's) also violates the i.i.d. assumption. So √t is the baseline under random-walk assumptions; real markets deviate, which is itself a source of signals.

problems.title: Gambler's ruin / hitting probability
problems.statement: You start with $k and repeatedly bet $1 on a fair coin (win or lose $1 each flip, p=0.5). You stop when you reach $0 (ruin) or $N (target). What is the probability you reach $N before $0? Solve it (a symmetric random walk on {0,…,N}) and state how the answer changes if the game is slightly unfavorable.
problems.hint: For a fair walk, the hitting probability is linear in the start position. Use the martingale / optional-stopping argument.
problems.tests: Random walk hitting probabilities via martingale reasoning.

approach: For a fair game, your bankroll is a martingale (expected change per bet = 0). By the Optional Stopping Theorem, the expected bankroll at the stopping time equals the start: E[final] = k. The final value is either 0 (with prob 1−P) or N (with prob P), so N·P + 0·(1−P) = k ⇒ P = k/N. The probability of reaching the target $N before ruin is simply k/N — linear in your starting wealth. (E.g., start with $30, target $100: P = 30/100 = 30%.)
Intuition/derivation alternative: let f(k) = P(reach N before 0 | start k). The fair-walk recurrence f(k) = ½f(k−1) + ½f(k+1) with f(0)=0, f(N)=1 has the linear solution f(k)=k/N.

If the game is slightly unfavorable (win prob p<0.5, lose prob q=1−p), the answer becomes exponential rather than linear: P = (1−(q/p)^k)/(1−(q/p)^N), which is much smaller than k/N even for a tiny edge against you — and as the number of bets grows, ruin becomes nearly certain. This is the mathematical reason a small house edge (or paying the spread/fees every trade) compounds against you, and why bet sizing and a real positive edge matter: with no edge you have a fair k/N shot, but with a persistent negative edge the exponential term crushes you. It's the flip side of why HFT wants a small *positive* edge repeated many times rather than a fair game.
